name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
title: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
answer: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers methods for research institutions to jointly analyze or train models on restricted datasets without moving raw records to a central repository. Sensitive data in this context includes health records, financial details, personal identifiers, and other regulated or confidential research material. The scope includes technical protocols, data use agreements, and repository practices that allow cross-institutional collaboration while keeping each dataset under its home institution's control.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers methods for research institutions to jointly analyze or train models on restricted datasets without moving raw records to a central repository. Sensitive data in this context includes health records, financial details, personal identifiers, and other regulated or confidential research material. The scope includes technical protocols, data use agreements, and repository practices that allow cross-institutional collaboration while keeping each dataset under its home institution's control.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a network of local nodes at each data holder, connected to a coordination server that receives only model updates or aggregate statistics. Secure aggregation, encrypted channels, and trusted execution environments are common components, along with differential privacy mechanisms that add calibrated noise to shared outputs. Some deployments use federated learning frameworks and secure multi-party computation libraries, but the core requirement is that raw sensitive data never leaves the source infrastructure.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Each participating site computes a local model update or summary statistic on its own data, then sends only that update to a central aggregator. The aggregator combines updates from all sites, often using secure aggregation so that individual contributions cannot be inspected, and returns a global model or result. Techniques such as homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, and differential privacy protect the shared updates from revealing individual records. Data provenance is maintained through logs that record which dataset version contributed to each round of computation.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk are managed through data use agreements, institutional review board approvals, and consent frameworks that specify what each party may compute and share. Residual risks include inference attacks, model inversion, and re-identification from aggregate outputs, so repositories track provenance metadata and access logs for audit. Governance practice focuses on limiting the information content of shared updates and ensuring that each data holder retains authority over its own records, rather than transferring ownership or custody to a central party.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Federated sharing is moving toward standardized protocols and interoperability across different repository software and research domains. Future work is likely to extend beyond model training to federated analytics, cohort discovery, and verifiable computation, with stronger guarantees from zero-knowledge proofs and formal privacy accounting. Repositories are also expected to integrate federated methods with trusted research environments and automated data use agreement enforcement, reducing manual overhead while preserving auditability.
